full_title: On Statistical Methods for Genetics: Fisher, Ewens and the Bayesian Programme
short_description: Statistical theory of population genetics: an exact form of Fisher's Fundamental Theorem, shrinkage estimates of the rate of adaptation, the Ewens sampling formula and its rigidity, rational conjugacy, and sufficiency for learned coalescent inference.
description:
This book treats the mathematical theory of population genetics as a problem in statistical inference, from Fisher's Fundamental Theorem of Natural Selection to learned inference for the coalescent.

It shows that Fisher's decomposition of the rate of change of mean fitness holds for arbitrary genotype frequencies, with an exact remainder computed for one and two loci. It shows that the usual plug in estimate of the additive genetic variance is inflated by a term that grows with the number of loci, and that shrinkage under a horseshoe prior gives a conservative correction. It derives the Ewens sampling formula from de Finetti's theorem, proves that among sampling weights only power weights preserve the residual allocation structure of Poisson Dirichlet subdivisions, and leaves the case of general weights as a stated conjecture. It develops rational conjugacy for Pochhammer priors on concentration parameters, with exact residue formulas for normalizing constants and Zipf tails for the counts they generate. For inference without a likelihood it proves that a learned quantile map that attains the Bayes risk is sufficient, that the number of segregating sites is not sufficient for the mutation rate, and that DeepSets encoders see only the site frequency spectrum.

The book is written for statisticians and mathematical biologists with graduate level probability. Numerical results are labelled as computations where they rest on simulation.

chapters.title: A Short History of Population Genetics
chapters.summary:
This chapter is a history of population genetics told through the statistical questions each period left open. It follows Darwin's difficulty with blending inheritance, Mendel's ratios and their chi square test, the quarrel between the biometricians and the Mendelians, and the synthesis of Fisher, Haldane and Wright. It then covers Kimura's diffusions and the neutral theory, the sampling theory of Ewens and Kingman, the coalescent, and the genomic era of biobanks and polygenic traits. Six worked examples use numbers small enough to check by hand: Mendel's 3 to 1 ratio, the Hardy Weinberg law, Fisher's decomposition of the genetic variance, Haldane's 2s, the Ewens sampling formula and the expected times of the coalescent. The chapter proves no new theorem. Its purpose is to set the questions that the later chapters take up: what the Fundamental Theorem of Natural Selection says and what it costs, how many parameters a genomic model really has, how neutral alleles are sampled, and how to infer without a likelihood.

#### From the literature

The chapter presents work of Darwin, Mendel, Fisher, Haldane, Wright, Kimura, Ewens and Kingman, with the dates and names given in the text. The Hardy Weinberg law is due to Hardy (1908) and Weinberg (1908). Ewens's sampling formula is Ewens (1972) and the coalescent is Kingman (1982).

chapters.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Natural Selection: From Deterministic to Stochastic, Fisher to Bayes
chapters.summary:
Fisher's Fundamental Theorem of Natural Selection says that the additive genetic variance is the rate of change of mean fitness. As a statement about the total change it is false, as Kimura showed in 1958 and as Ewens (2024) sets out. This chapter asks what the falsehood costs and what replaces it. The deterministic half rests on a lemma: the average effects are the coefficients of an orthogonal projection of fitness onto a fixed subspace taken in a moving inner product. The result is an exact decomposition of the rate of change of mean fitness into Fisher's additive term and a remainder, valid for arbitrary frequency paths and for the whole genome. The remainder vanishes for every fitness assignment exactly when the log frequencies move inside the span of the gene contents. The chapter gives the remainder in closed form at one biallelic locus and at two loci, an exact remainder and relative error for one locus with k alleles, and a factorization when the distribution moves in an exponential family. The stochastic half asks what data can say about Fisher's claim, using Bayes factors and global local shrinkage.

#### From the literature

Fisher (1930) stated the theorem. Price (1972) and Ewens (1989) gave the reading in terms of the partial change in mean fitness, and Kimura (1958) gave the counterexample to the total change reading. Ewens (2024) is the account the chapter builds on. Lindley (1988) supplies the coordinates used for the biallelic remainder.

#### New results

- [Moving projection lemma](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#moving_projection_lemma) (Lemma 3.2, page 63; proved): For arbitrary smooth genotype frequency paths the rate of change of mean Malthusian fitness is Fisher's additive term plus a remainder that pairs the least squares deviations with the logarithmic velocity of the genotype frequencies. New in this book.
- [Whole genome Fundamental Theorem decomposition](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#whole_genome) (Theorem 3.5, page 66; proved): For arbitrary genotype frequency paths, the rate of change of mean Malthusian fitness splits exactly into an additive part and a remainder; the remainder vanishes whenever the log frequencies move inside the span of the gene contents, and it vanishes for every assignment of fitnesses only then. New in this book.
- [Exponential family factorization of the remainder](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#exponential_family_factorization) (Theorem 3.8, page 69; proved): When the genotype distribution moves inside an exponential family whose main effects are the gene contents, the main effects contribute nothing to the remainder, which depends on the interaction coordinates alone. New in this book.
- [Remainder in Lindley coordinates](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#remainder_in_lindley_coordinates) (Corollary 3.10, page 70; proved): At a biallelic locus, in the coordinates of allele frequency and Hardy Weinberg disequilibrium, the remainder is the dominance contrast times the Fisher information times the velocity of the disequilibrium coefficient. New in this book.
- [The residual in closed form at a biallelic locus](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#the_residual_in_closed_form) (Proposition 3.11, page 71; proved): At a biallelic locus the residual of the additive projection is one known vector times one number, which gives the dominance variance and the remainder in closed form. New in this book.
- [Two locus residual](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#two_locus_residual) (Proposition 3.14, page 73; proved): For two biallelic loci the residual is an interaction contrast times the information about linkage disequilibrium, so recombination alone changes mean fitness at an exact rate. New in this book.
- [Exact remainder for one locus with k alleles](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#exact_remainder_one_locus_alleles) (Theorem 3.16, page 76; proved): In the one locus random mating model with constant fitnesses, the change in mean fitness is the additive term divided by mean fitness plus an explicit quadratic remainder in the dominance deviations. New in this book.
- [Exact relative error of the Fundamental Theorem, two alleles](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#exact_relative_error_two_alleles) (Corollary 3.17, page 76; proved): At a biallelic locus the relative size of the remainder against the additive term is exactly D pq divided by twice mean fitness, which is first order in the selection coefficient. chapters.title: The Horseshoe and the Fundamental Theorem of Natural Selection
chapters.summary:
This chapter reads the Fundamental Theorem through estimation. Once the average effects are the coefficients of a weighted least squares regression of genotypic fitness on allelic dosage, the theorem is an algebraic identity and its empirical content becomes the estimation of a regression with more loci than individuals. The plug in estimate of the additive variance is then inflated by the number of loci times the noise variance over the sample size, and the implied rate of adaptation is overstated. The chapter estimates the average effects under a horseshoe prior and reads the theorem through the shrinkage weights. Three results are proved: any shrinkage rule gives a conservative estimate of the additive variance; oracle shrinkage tuned for the average effects necessarily understates it; and the coherent estimator is the posterior mean of the quadratic functional, not the quadratic of the posterior mean. A simulation with 400 loci and 300 individuals reports the naive estimator, ridge and the horseshoe, and the chapter then treats the secondary theorem, bilinear and general quadratic forms with linkage disequilibrium, truncation on measured fitness, and ascertainment of survivors.

#### From the literature

The partial change reading of the theorem is due to Price (1972) and Ewens (1989), with the account of Ewens and Lessard (2015). Fisher (1930) is the original. The horseshoe prior is Carvalho, Polson and Scott (2010). The secondary theorem is Robertson's.

#### New results

- [Bias of the plug in estimate of additive variance](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#bias_of_the_plug_in) (Proposition 4.4, page 133; proved): With orthogonal columns, the plug in estimator of the additive variance is inflated by the number of loci times the noise variance over the sample size. New in this book.
- [Shrinkage is conservative](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#shrinkage_is_conservative) (Proposition 4.9, page 139; proved): Any shrinkage weights give an estimate of the additive variance no larger than the plug in estimate. New in this book.
- [Oracle shrinkage understates the additive variance](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#oracle_shrinkage_understates_the_additive_variance) (Proposition 4.10, page 140; proved): Shrinkage tuned to estimate each average effect as well as possible necessarily understates the additive variance, by an explicit amount. New in this book.
- [The coherent estimator is the posterior mean of the quadratic](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#the_coherent_estimator) (Proposition 4.11, page 141; proved): The posterior mean of the additive variance is the sum of the squared posterior means plus the posterior variances, so it is never below the plug in of the posterior means. New in this book.

#### Key terms

Fundamental Theorem of Natural Selection, horseshoe prior, shrinkage, rate of adaptation, additive genetic variance estimation, whole genome regression, p greater than n, plug in bias, oracle shrinkage, Robertson secondary theorem, truncation selection, ascertainment, linkage disequilibrium, quadratic functional

chapters.title: Many Parameter Models in Population Genetics
chapters.summary:
Population genetics has become a many parameter subject, and this chapter asks what that does to the quantities of the Fundamental Theorem. Fisher's average effect, as restated by Ewens (2024), is a weighted least squares projection. The plug in additive variance from a linear smoother carries a noise term, which for the unregularised fit is an inflation of exactly p sigma squared over N, and the inflation stops growing at the interpolation threshold. The natural prior for such problems is a species sampling prior. The chapter proves that the Beta law of the horseshoe shrinkage weight is the law of the first stick breaking weight of a two parameter GEM family, which ties shrinkage to the Ewens Pitman partition. It derives the allele frequency spectrum induced by a shrinkage prior, Fisher's log series as the special case, and the effective model size, whose growth rate matches the number of species under the matching Poisson Dirichlet law with constants that differ by a factor between about 0.89 and 1. The two constructions fluctuate differently: the shrinkage count concentrates while the species count has a Mittag Leffler limit.

#### From the literature

The Hoppe urn is Hoppe (1984). The Poisson Kingman partition formula and the Pitman Yor size biased results are due to Pitman and to Pitman and Yor (1997). Ewens's sufficiency of the number of alleles is Ewens (1972). The horseshoe is Carvalho, Polson and Scott (2010).

#### New results

- [Inflation of Fisher's fitted projection](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#inflation_of_fishers_fitted_projection) (Corollary 5.6, page 167; proved): The unregularized fit of the projection that defines the average effects inflates the estimated additive variance by exactly the number of parameters times the noise variance over the sample size. New in this book.
- [Saturation of the optimism past the interpolation threshold](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#saturation_of_the_optimism) (Corollary 5.10, page 174; proved): The inflation of the fitted additive variance grows linearly in the number of parameters up to the sample size and is constant afterwards. New in this book.
- [Shrinkage weights are stick breaking weights](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#shrinkage_weights_are_stick_breaking_weights) (Theorem 5.15, page 180; proved): The Beta law of the horseshoe type shrinkage weight is exactly the law of the first stick breaking weight of the two parameter GEM family, which links shrinkage priors to Ewens Pitman partitions. New in this book.
- [Spectrum and shrinkage profile](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#spectrum_and_shrinkage_profile) (Theorem 5.18, page 181; proved): The mean intensity of the atoms of a random discrete distribution is the density of a size biased pick divided by x, which gives the expected allele frequency spectrum of a shrinkage prior from the density of its shrinkage weight. New in this book.
- [Discovery rates of shrinkage priors](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#discovery_rates_of_shrinkage_priors) (Corollary 5.22, page 182; proved): A global local prior with a Beta shrinkage weight discovers a number of signals that grows like a power of the sample size, n to the one half for the horseshoe, or only logarithmically when a equals one. New in this book.
- [Effective model size of a shrinkage prior](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#effective_model_size) (Theorem 5.23, page 183; proved): The expected number of coefficients that survive the penalty grows like a power of the sample size, or like a logarithm when a equals one, at the canonical global scale. New in this book.
- [Rates agree between effective model size and number of species](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#the_rates_agree_and_the_constants_nearly_do) (Corollary 5.24, page 183; proved): The growth rates of the effective model size and of the expected number of blocks under the matching Poisson Dirichlet law are the same, and the constants differ by a factor between about 0.89 and 1. New in this book.
- [The shrinkage count and the species count fluctuate differently](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#the_two_constructions_fluctuate_differently) (Proposition 5.27, page 186; proved): The effective model size concentrates around its mean while the number of blocks under the Pitman Yor partition has a nondegenerate random limit. New in this book.

chapters.title: The Ewens Sampling Formula by de Finetti's Theorem
chapters.summary:
This chapter derives the Ewens sampling formula from de Finetti's theorem in the elementary form of Heath and Sudderth, where the mixing measure is a weak limit of the laws of the empirical distribution function. Helly selection and the Helly Bray lemma give the representation, and the only inequality needed is that drawing k items with and without replacement from n differs by k(k-1)/(2n) in total variation. If the one step forecast depends on the past only through the empirical distribution and is affine in it, exchangeability forces the weights theta over theta plus n and n over theta plus n, and the directing measure is a Dirichlet process. The chapter gives an exact finite sample variance and a moment estimator of theta, the exchangeable partition probability function, the sufficiency of the number of alleles and its law, and moments of the abundance counts. It then weights the paintbox by abundance, shows that the de Finetti architecture is invariant, treats the two parameter Pitman family including its negative branch as a finite allele model, and applies the tools to Corbet's butterflies, with the fit corrected for the censoring of the collection.

#### From the literature

De Finetti's theorem in the elementary form is Heath and Sudderth (1976). The Ewens sampling formula is Ewens (1972). Kingman's paintbox is Kingman (1978). Pitman's sampling formula is Pitman (1995). Corbet's butterfly data are from Fisher, Corbet and Williams (1943). The finite allele reading of the negative branch is classical.

#### New results

- [Exchangeability forces the Ewens predictive weights](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#the_weights_are_forced) (Proposition 6.8, page 217; proved): If the one step forecast is affine in the empirical distribution and the sequence is exchangeable, the weights are theta over theta plus n and n over theta plus n. New in this book.
- [Exact finite n variance and a moment estimator of theta](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#exact_finite_variance_and_a_moment_estimator) (Proposition 6.11, page 219; proved): The variance of an empirical average under the Ewens predictive rule is exact for every n and can be inverted to give theta without any asymptotic approximation. New in this book.
- [The de Finetti architecture is invariant under abundance weighting](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#the_de_finetti_architecture_is_invariant) (Proposition 6.23, page 233; proved): Weighting the sampling probabilities by a function of abundance keeps the sample exchangeable and changes only the mixing measure. New in this book.
- [The negative branch is not a weighted paintbox](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#the_negative_branch_is_not_a_weighted_paintbox) (Proposition 6.34, page 239; proved): A two parameter partition law with negative discount cannot be reproduced by weighting a one parameter Poisson Dirichlet paintbox. New in this book.

#### Key terms

chapters.title: Ascertainment and the Two Parameter Poisson Dirichlet Family
chapters.summary:
Sampling a Poisson Dirichlet subdivision of the unit interval with a nonuniform density is a weighted distribution problem for Kingman's paintbox. In the one parameter case it has an exact answer: a Beta(1, alpha) weight carries the Ewens sampling formula with parameter theta to the one with parameter theta over alpha. This chapter asks what survives in the two parameter family. The reduction survives. Exactness does not, and the obstruction is a rigidity theorem: the residual allocation structure is preserved only by power weights, and among power weights the Ewens family alone is preserved, so no sampling density that charges every interval carries the size biased sticks of PD(sigma, theta) with sigma positive to another member. No Kingman type genealogy in which the mutation probability depends only on the branch count can give the family either. The chapter classifies the growth of the number of types under a general weight by its behaviour at the origin, shows that the abundance spectrum degenerates, and proves that the singleton fraction estimates the exponent with an explicit bias.

#### From the literature

Kingman's paintbox is Kingman (1978). The Ewens Pitman family and its sampling formula are due to Pitman and to Pitman and Yor (1997). The one parameter reduction by a Beta weight is as stated in the chapter. Karlin's occupancy correspondence is used as cited there.

#### New results

- [Closure of the Ewens Pitman family under weighted sampling](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#py_thm_pitman) (Theorem 7.9, page 269; proved): Sampling a two parameter Poisson Dirichlet population in the size biased layout with a power density keeps the Ewens Pitman family closed only in the Ewens case or when the density is uniform. New in this book.
- [Rigidity of the residual allocation structure](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#py_thm_rigid) (Theorem 7.11, page 271; proved): Among sampling densities that charge every interval, only power weights keep the induced subdivision of the size biased layout a residual allocation model, so for a discount strictly between zero and one no such density other than the uniform one carries a two parameter Poisson Dirichlet law to the stick breaking sequence of another member of the family. New in this book.
- [No Kingman type genealogy produces the two parameter family](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#py_prop_nocoal) (Proposition 7.12, page 273; proved): A genealogy in which the mutation probability depends only on the number of branches gives a count of types with variance at most its mean, which rules out positive discount. New in this book.
- [Exponent map of the number of types under power sampling](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#exponent_map_under_power_sampling) (Proposition 7.13, page 275; proved): Sampling a Poisson Dirichlet population in the size biased layout with a power density gives an exact power law envelope and moves the growth exponent of the number of types from sigma to sigma star. New in this book.
- [The sigma diversity is a power of the stick envelope](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#sigma_diversity_is_a_power_of_the_stick_envelope) (Lemma 7.16, page 279; proved): The almost sure limit of the number of types over n to the sigma equals the sigma th power of the stick envelope constant over sigma, with no constant left over. New in this book.
- [The weighted diversity is a power of the unweighted diversity](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#diversity_is_a_power_of_the_unweighted_diversity) (Proposition 7.17, page 280; proved): Under power sampling the limit of the number of types over n to the sigma star is a constant times a power of the unweighted sigma diversity. New in this book.
- [The constant in the diversity power law](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#constant_in_the_diversity_power_law) (Proposition 7.18, page 280; proved): The constant relating the weighted and unweighted diversities has a closed form in gamma functions, does not depend on theta, and equals one for uniform sampling. - [Bias of the singleton fraction](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#py_prop_rate) (Proposition 7.27, page 288; proved): Under an exact power law envelope with exponent sigma star, the expected singleton fraction exceeds sigma star by a relative amount of one over twice the expected number of types. chapters.title: Pólya Inverse Gamma Posteriors, Fisher's Species Model, and Good's Predictive Rule for the Ewens Sampling Problem
chapters.summary:
This chapter gives an inferential account of Fisher's species model, the Ewens sampling formula and Good's predictive rule, connected by Polya inverse gamma augmentation. The Ewens richness likelihood is a regular one parameter natural exponential family in log theta with sufficient statistic K, the number of species, so the maximum likelihood equation is pure moment matching. A Bernstein von Mises argument shows that the Bayes estimator agrees with the maximum likelihood estimate to relative order one over K and the credible interval with the Wald interval, so in this sense the Bayes estimator of theta adds little. Fisher's two parameters map onto the two PIG representations: the richness needs only the gamma ratio block, and the shape that governs departure from the log series needs the full PIG(0) engine. Good's estimator, once given the Ewens model, is the Ewens predictive rule, and the predictive law of the number of new species is a sum of independent Bernoulli variables. The posterior of theta has a Pareto tail under an improper flat prior, which limits its moments. A three block Gibbs sampler is given.

#### From the literature

Fisher, Corbet and Williams (1943) introduced the index of diversity and the log series. Good (1953) and Good and Toulmin (1956) asked the predictive questions. McCullagh (2016) shows that Fisher's two parameter Poisson process contains the Ewens law. Polya inverse gamma augmentation is He, Polson and Xu (2019). The Ewens sampling formula is Ewens (1972).

#### New results

- [Inverse gamma series for PIG(0)](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#inverse_gamma_series_for_pig0) (Proposition 8.7, page 313; proved): The Polya Inverse Gamma variable that turns a reciprocal gamma factor into a Gaussian kernel is an explicit series of independent inverse gamma variables, with finite mean and infinite variance. New in this book.
- [Good's rule is the Ewens predictive](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#goods_rule_is_the_ewens_predictive) (Proposition 8.9, page 316; proved): Under the Ewens model, Good's predictive probability for a species seen r times is r over n plus theta, and the unseen mass is theta over n plus theta. New in this book.
- [Predictive law of the number of new species](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#predictive_law_of_new_species) (Proposition 8.11, page 317; proved): The number of new species in m further specimens is a sum of independent Bernoulli variables given theta, with explicit mean and variance in terms of the digamma function. New in this book.
- [Asymptotic redundancy of the Bayes estimator of theta](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#asymptotic_redundancy) (Proposition 8.13, page 319; proved): For the Ewens richness likelihood, the posterior of the log concentration is asymptotically normal, and the Bayes estimator and credible interval agree with the maximum likelihood estimator and Wald interval to leading order. New in this book.
- [Tail of the concentration posterior](https://vsokolov.org/books/statistical_methods_genetics/results.html#tail_of_the_concentration_posterior) (Proposition 8.15, page 321; proved): Under a gamma type prior with no exponential decay, the posterior of theta has a Pareto tail, so its moments exist only when the number of species is small enough. New in this book.
